meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A man who has never gone to school may steal from a freight car; but if he has a university education, he may steal the whole railroad'?
meta.ogDescription: Pinned on Theodore Roosevelt, but unsourced: the earliest printing we can find is 1945, 26 years after his death.

answer.label: Not Theodore Roosevelt — an unsourced 20th-century saying
answer.sourceLine: No source in Roosevelt’s own writing or speeches has ever been produced for this line. Wikiquote files it under “Disputed” ↗ and traces it no further back than a 1952 textbook. Searching the Library of Congress newspaper archive ourselves pushes it earlier — to a Veterans of Foreign Wars newsletter of 1 March 1945 ↗ — but that is still 26 years after Roosevelt died, and it is already credited to him there.

source.heading: Where the line actually surfaces

docMeta.dd: Monthly News of the Department of Washington (Veterans of Foreign Wars), 1 March 1945
Art of Communicating Ideas (1952) by William Joseph Grace, p. 389

source.excerpt: It was President Theodore Roosevelt who observed, “A man who has never gone to school may steal from a freight car; but if he has a university education, he may steal the whole railroad.”
trail: Wikiquote lists the line under “Disputed” ↗ on its Theodore Roosevelt page, citing only Art of Communicating Ideas (1952) by William Joseph Grace, p. 389 — a textbook published 33 years after Roosevelt’s death.

Searching the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America newspaper archive for the line’s distinctive wording returns only two pages ↗ — the Peninsula Enterprise, 22 September 1950 ↗ and the Nome Nugget, 18 February 1963 ↗. Nothing from Roosevelt’s lifetime, which ended 6 January 1919.

Widening the search to “may steal the whole railroad” adds one earlier page: the V.F.W. Monthly News of 1 March 1945 ↗, which already prints the line over Roosevelt’s name. That is the earliest attributed appearance we could locate — 26 years after he died, and seven years before the citation Wikiquote gives.

The wording appears nowhere in the seven Roosevelt books we searched on Project Gutenberg — including his Autobiography ↗, The Strenuous Life ↗ and his complete State of the Union addresses ↗ — roughly 3.8 MB of text searched for both “freight car” and “college education”, with no match.
source.excerptNote: How the line actually circulated: a filler paragraph in The Nome Nugget (Alaska), 18 February 1963 ↗, printed between that week’s ten best-selling records and a birthday-punch recipe. The earliest printing we found is 18 years older — the 1 March 1945 V.F.W. newsletter ↗ — but its scan is badly mis-read by OCR, so this cleaner 1963 copy is quoted instead.

source.rightsNote: The wording cannot be tied to any identified author or first publication, so no copyright or public-domain status is asserted here. The mid-century newspaper printings quoted above are evidence of circulation, not of authorship.

author.name: Theodore Roosevelt
author.heading: About the credited author
author.bio: Theodore Roosevelt was president from 1901 to 1909, the youngest ever to take the office, and built his reputation on trust-busting, conservation and a talent for the quotable phrase. That talent is precisely why unsourced aphorisms drift onto his name — he wrote and spoke enough, and vividly enough, that almost anything punchy about power or character sounds like him. His verified output runs to millions of words, and this line is in none of it.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly credited to
misattribution.intro: This is a clean example of an orphan aphorism finding a famous father: a sharp line about education and white-collar crime, and a president remembered for going after the trusts. The fit is good. The evidence is absent.

items.why: Nothing in his books, letters or speeches contains it, and no printing survives from his lifetime. Wikiquote ↗ classes the attribution as disputed; the earliest copy we could find already credits him, in 1945 ↗, 26 years after his death.

Both surviving early copies are anonymous space-fillers — the V.F.W. newsletter ↗ sets it beside a membership table and two jokes, the Nome Nugget ↗ beside a pop chart. Filler columns repeat sayings; they do not originate or verify them.

misattribution.truthLine: On the evidence available, this is an anonymous mid-twentieth-century saying that acquired Roosevelt’s name somewhere before 1945. If you must quote it, quote it as unattributed — Wikiquote’s disputed listing ↗ is the honest citation.

context.heading: Why the confusion
lead: Roosevelt is one of the internet’s great quote magnets, and for a reason: he really did say a great many quotable things about wealth, corporations and public morals, so a new line in that register sounds like something he would have said. That plausibility is exactly what makes an attribution hard to dislodge.

The joke itself may well be older than any of its surviving printings — sayings usually are, and this one arrives in 1945 with no sign of being new. What cannot be shown is that Roosevelt ever put it this way, or at all.
detailsBody: The search that matters here is the negative one. Chronicling America covers American newspapers across Roosevelt’s entire public life, and he was among the most quoted men alive; a line this repeatable should leave traces while he was saying it. It leaves none until 1945.

OCR on old newsprint is imperfect, so absence is not proof — a badly scanned page could hide an earlier copy. But the pattern is the familiar one for a misattribution: no lifetime record, then a sudden appearance in quotation books and filler columns decades later, name already attached.
context.pull: The fit is good. The evidence is absent.
